text: Lesson 34 ended with a decision: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, on a single GPU, for Anchorline Systems' internal support assistant. This lesson stands that decision up as a running service — the deployment architecture, a real vLLM launch command, and the smoke test that proves it actually works.

Even a one-GPU deployment has more pieces than just "run the model." Client applications — the Slack integration and the internal tool — send chat requests to an API gateway, which terminates TLS and would route across replicas if this ever scaled past one GPU. The gateway hands off to the vLLM server, an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server that owns the model, the KV cache, and the request scheduler. And underneath all of it sits the GPU, where continuous batching and PagedAttention from chapter four actually do their work.

Standing it up is pip install vllm, then vllm serve pointed at meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with a handful of real flags: bfloat16 precision, a max model length of 8192 tokens, 90 percent GPU memory utilization, a max of 64 sequences per batch, and chunked prefill enabled.

Each of those flags is a decision, not boilerplate. Capping context at 8K rather than the model's full 128K frees up KV-cache memory, because Anchorline's requests are a question plus some pasted logs, not a 128K-token document. Ninety percent GPU memory utilization sets how much of the card vLLM can claim for weights and cache. Max num seqs 64 is the ceiling on continuous batching from lesson 19. And chunked prefill means one long prompt doesn't stall everyone else's decode steps. Notice what's missing: there's no flag to turn on continuous batching or PagedAttention — those are vLLM's defaults. You're tuning how aggressively they run, not switching them on.

Before trusting it with real traffic, smoke-test it against the OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint with curl — a real response with the expected structure confirms the model loaded, the scheduler is accepting requests, and KV cache allocation succeeded.

A thin stack, with every meaningful decision living in the launch flags, built on defaults you already understand. Next up, Lesson 36: benchmarking this exact deployment honestly, and tuning it based on what the numbers say.
